criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking and domestic water supply service access in the municipality of Queimados (Rio de Janeiro Metropolitan Region), comparing public piped network access (CEDAE) with reliance on informal natural water springs and private wells across two neighbourhoods (Jardim da Fonte and Vila do Rosário).
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain=yes -> plain_criterion2_decision='include') but fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (narrow=no -> decision='exclude', E03). Under the plain broad wording, the qualitative interviews and triangulation examine governance and politico-institutional factors including centralized metropolitan utility management by CEDAE, core-periphery infrastructure investment neglect, clientelism/patronage, lack of clear institutional accountability for monitoring spring water quality, and informal/formal service co-production. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, the paper does not empirically examine a rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, frontline discretion or accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory rules directly governing access). In the survey/MCA, the exposure is physical presence vs absence of public piped infrastructure across two neighbourhoods, while the qualitative analysis studies spontaneous, unorganized grassroots spring collection coexisting ('spotted zebra' socio-technical hybridity) with an intermittent centralized network, treating political culture, clientelism, and broad institutional centralization/fragmentation (including only a single passing sentence noting a 30-year municipal delegation contract to CEDAE) as socio-technical and macro-governance background rather than an analysed rule-type access mechanism.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical mixed-methods case study combining a 2014 field survey of 90 natural spring users analysed via Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA) with 9 in-depth semi-structured interviews (3 key informants, 3 CEDAE officials/technicians, and 3 local community representatives) analysed via inductive coding and triangulation.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports outcomes directly relevant to household water access and service availability/reliability, including household connection to the public piped network (55% connected among spring users; connected in JdF vs unconnected in VdR), possession of private wells, frequency of spring water collection, types of domestic water use, and perceived vs microbiological water quality.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (90 surveyed individual spring users/households at two natural springs plus 9 institutional/community interviewees in Queimados), study exposure (physical piped network presence/absence and informal-formal socio-technical coexistence), access/use outcomes, and mixed-methods case-study design are clearly reported.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English, an eligible language without translation.

study_design: Exploratory mixed-methods case study (field survey of n = 90 users analysed with Multiple Correspondence Analysis and n = 9 semi-structured interviews analysed via inductive coding and triangulation)
population_and_sample: Natural spring water users in two neighbourhoods (Jardim da Fonte and Vila do Rosário) of Queimados, Rio de Janeiro Metropolitan Region, Brazil (non-probabilistic survey sample of n = 90 spring users; plus n = 9 semi-structured interviews with public-sector key informants, CEDAE utility staff, and community representatives).
exposure: Socio-technical coexistence ('hybrid system') between incomplete/intermittent centralized public piped infrastructure and informal grassroots self-supply from natural springs across neighbourhoods with and without public network coverage, embedded in broad politico-institutional centralization and clientelist political culture.
outcome: Household connection to the public water network, reliance on private wells and natural springs, frequency of spring water collection, domestic water use types, and perceived/microbiological water quality.
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. Although this empirical mixed-methods case study examines household water supply access in Queimados, Brazil (c1=yes, c3=yes, c4=yes, c5=yes, c6=yes) and discusses broad governance, clientelism, institutional fragmentation, and centralized metropolitan utility management (passing the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 -> plain_criterion2_decision='include'), it does not empirically examine a legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, frontline discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or specific utility ownership/regulatory rules governing household access). Instead, the empirical analysis focuses on physical presence/absence of piped network infrastructure across two neighbourhoods and spontaneous household coping via unorganized natural spring water collection ('hybrid' socio-technical systems), treating political culture and institutional centralization as macro-governance background.
